newsitem.title: USA: Consumer confidence seen stable in 1997.
newsitem.headline: Consumer confidence seen stable in 1997.

text.p: Buoyed by strong job prospects, Americans continue to hold an optimistic view of the economy, which should lead to at least another year of favorable spending on homes and light vehicles, a University of Michigan consumer outlook showed Thursday.

Consumers expect unemployment to remain low, inflation to stay in check and remain unconcerned about their current debt loads as they approach 1997, said Richard Curtin, director of the university's Surveys of Consumers, which publishes a closely watched monthly consumer confidence guide.
"We can certainly expect one more year of growth," Curtin said during a presentation at the university's 44th annual Conference on the Economic Outlook.

The average for the consumer sentiment index so far this year is 92.7, up slightly from the 92.3 average in 1995 and the 92.2 average in 1994, Curtin said. The nearly three years in a row with the index in the low 90s rivals the level of optimism of the 1980s, he said.

Consumers do not forsee a huge surge in their fortunes, Curtin noted. Rather, their generally upbeat mood is based on more than five years of economic expansion and a belief that things will stay the same.
"The only concern that consumers have when they look ahead is they expect interest rates to rise. But at this point, they expect the increase to be rather modest," he said.
Except for interest rate expectations, Curtin's findings are in line with the annual economic forecast for 1997-98 delivered by University of Michigan Professor Saul Hymans.

According to Hymans, the U.S. economy will expand at moderate rate of 2.4 percent in 1997 and 2.3 percent in 1998, essentially unchanged from the 2.5 percent growth forecast for the fourth quarter of 1996. Consumer prices are seen rising two percent and 2.4 percent over the next two years.

Unemployment is forecast to be 5.3 percent next year and 5.4 percent in 1998, compared with 5.2 percent in October. The slight rise is based on an assumption that productivity will improve by 1.7 percent compared with a sub-par 0.6 percent rise this year, Hymans said, as fewer workers are required to obtain the same amount of output.

Hymans sees relatively little change in short and long-term interest rates over the next two years. The biggest danger ahead, he believes, is if productivity continues to lag. If that occurs and total demand continues to grow, Hymans said higher wage costs could lead to higher prices and an increase in inflation, prompting the Federal Reserve to raise interest rates.
--light vehicle sales of 15 million in 1997 and 15.1 million in 1998, compared to an expected 15.1 million in 1996;
--real disposable income growth of 3.1 percent next year and 2.4 percent in 1998;
--a 1.5 percent depreciation in the value of the dollar by 1998.
